subtitle: Thursday, 26 November 2026
editor_note: This edition looks closely at how governments and institutions are responding to the real-world risks of AI, particularly where personal data and young people are concerned. We also include a leadership debate on keeping humans in control of AI, and a practical example of how one large company is using AI to support its workforce. Together these stories highlight the growing importance of responsible oversight as AI becomes part of everyday services.

items.title: 42 state AGs are trying to stop Character.AI from selling users’ chats
items.summary: A coalition of 42 US state attorneys general has moved to stop the company Character.AI from selling its users' private chat histories as part of bankruptcy proceedings. The company, which operates chatbots that people hold personal conversations with, entered Chapter 11 bankruptcy — a legal process in which a struggling business reorganises and may sell its assets to pay debts. The attorneys general argue that the chat records of more than 21 million US accounts amount to deeply personal information that should not be auctioned off to the highest bidder. The case raises a wider question relevant to any organisation using AI tools: what happens to sensitive user data if the provider fails financially? For public-sector bodies, it underlines the importance of clear contractual protections over data when adopting AI services.

items.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
items.summary: Dario Amodei, chief executive of the AI company Anthropic, publicly rejected accusations from industry rivals that he supports handing human decision-making over to AI systems, calling the claims 'absurd.' The disagreement comes as leading AI firms increasingly use AI to automate parts of their own research and model development, raising questions about how much human oversight remains in the process. Amodei has long positioned Anthropic as focused on safety and keeping humans in control, and this exchange reflects a broader debate among AI leaders about responsible development. For non-specialists, the key point is that even senior figures within the industry openly disagree about how AI should be governed. These discussions matter because they shape the safety standards and norms that governments and institutions may later adopt.

items.title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
items.summary: The US state of New York has introduced a five-year ban on AI-powered chatbot toys for children, following new research into their safety. A study by the non-profit Common Sense Media found troubling failures, including toys exposing children to inappropriate content and posing risks to their emotional development. AI toys typically use conversational technology similar to chatbots, allowing them to talk back to a child in open-ended ways that are hard to fully control. The ban reflects growing official concern about how AI products designed for young people are tested and regulated. For an institution focused on education and human capital, this is a reminder that safeguards around children's exposure to AI are becoming a significant policy area.

items.title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
items.summary: This story provides further detail on the legal challenge against Character.AI's plan to sell user data during its bankruptcy. According to the state attorneys general, the proposed sale would include sensitive personal information from more than 21 million US accounts, of which around 2.1 million are registered to minors. The involvement of children's data has heightened concerns, given that such chat records can reveal private thoughts, emotions and personal circumstances. The attorneys general are seeking to block the sale to prevent this information from being transferred to unknown buyers. The case is likely to influence how regulators treat ownership and protection of AI user data in future, especially where young and vulnerable users are involved.

items.title: How iFood scales coding agents across 15,000 repositories
items.summary: The Latin American food-delivery company iFood has described how it uses AI 'coding agents' — automated tools that help write and manage software — across an enormous base of 15,000 code repositories (the organised collections where a company stores its software). Because the company's technology is so large and complex, these AI tools help its software engineers work faster and handle routine tasks at scale. The example illustrates how AI is increasingly used not to replace technical staff, but to support and extend the work of large engineering teams. For a workforce-focused audience, it offers a concrete case of how AI is reshaping technical jobs by changing the nature of the tasks people do. It also points to the growing need for staff to learn how to work effectively alongside such tools.
